findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity denials
findings.body: Check builds the denial-cache key from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder only; the identity type is not included. Supported subjects include anonymous:0 and render:0, both of which parse to the identifier "0". A denied check for anonymous will therefore write a denial entry that a subsequent renderer check with the same action/resource/folder will hit, causing the renderer to be denied even though renderer permissions are hard-coded to allow dashboard/folder/datasource reads. The reverse is also possible. The denial key should include the identity type.

findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and can collide across resources
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with underscores. Resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different (name, parent) tuples can produce the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="" and name="a" with parent="b" both serialize to the suffix "_a_b_". Because a denial-cache hit short-circuits the authorization check, a denial cached for one resource/folder combination can be incorrectly applied to another, causing authorized requests to be denied for the cache TTL. Use an unambiguous escaping, separator scheme, or hash of the fields.

findings.title: Cached denial can continue to deny after permissions are granted
findings.body: Check returns false immediately when a denial-cache entry exists, and denial entries are written after any failed full check with a 30-second TTL. If access is granted immediately after a denial, for example when permissions are added around dashboard/folder creation, subsequent checks for that exact resource will keep hitting the denial cache and will be denied until the TTL expires. This can still block access to newly created resources, which is the issue this PR is intended to fix. Consider invalidating negative entries on permission changes, avoiding negative caching in this path, or using a much shorter TTL.
